doc.title: Ada Rovatti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 13, 2022

title: Surprises and complexity in her compositions
summary: Her tunes contain twists and shifts of tempo; charts are complex and specific on the head.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Let me ask you about your composing. There’s two tunes that I heard and well I know they’re a number of years apart as far as your recordings. One was “Air Drop” and the
other one was “I Lost My Wisdom.” And they both have — if my memory serves me they both have a thing where you start out in one tempo and feel, before long you go somewhere else.

Yeah. That’s a thing I do in all my tunes there’s always a little — little things of surprise, little things that when you expect something happen or is not happening or when you don’t expect, you know you expect just smooth sailing for the rest of a tune something else happens to rock you. And I think that musicians at this point, the musicians I’m working with, they know when I bring new tunes they’re like oh here we are, what she’s doing. And I just like — I don’t know maybe I have a little attention disorder. So I like — I don’t want to get bored so that’s why I always throw a twist in my tunes it’s just kind of like oop! And I like to see the reaction of the musician because I remember one drummer told me it’s like as soon as you get in the groove and you’re thinking I got it, you throw something that I need to just keep an eye on my chart. You know I don’t want to sound like you know just do like a cycle that goes from one thing to the other. Like sometimes I write tunes that they sound very organic and then when you analyze the chart it’s like oh I didn’t realize you moved from 7/8 to da-da-da da-da-da. But your ears doesn’t feel it as just a change, a big change or a change of tempo or something like that. Only when you see the chart — that’s also sometimes things that — they almost have to see it enough with smooth jazz because I wouldn’t call smooth jazz my tunes but they say oh you know I have it, I got it down. And then when they see the music it’s like I guess I need to give an extra look to the chart. They sound —
Are your charts complicated? Would you call them complicated?

Yes they are. They don’t sound complicated but they are. And I tend, especially in the last couple recordings I started to become very — a little control freak — let’s say it like that. I like to write specific things: a bass line, voicing, specific rhythm and bass line, specific bass line through the melody. On the solo do whatever you want. I mean I leave you the freedom of going around. But on the head I want specific things and I have a clear mind. You know I just saw, the recording we did in Germany you know there were a couple of places that the band was like I don’t know, did you write this one? It was like no, I want it exactly like that. I don’t know if it works, it’s not the right key for the bass. No I wanted it — play it the way it’s written. And then they were like ha! It actually does work. I was like yeah. I hear it. You know I knew what I wanted. So I was excited that I stuck to my guns.
